title: ‘ALL TALK ON BUDGET REFORMS’: Budget watchdog seeks written House pledge to open 2027 bicam

 Privacy Policy Home > news NATION ‘ALL TALK ON BUDGET REFORMS’: Budget watchdog seeks written House pledge to open 2027 bicam
 4 min read Share full article 0 November 16, 2026 By Joseph Bernard A. Marzan
 ILOILO CITY — The People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) said the House of Representatives has yet to turn its promises to reform the 2027 national budget into concrete action, particularly a written guarantee that civil society groups and media can attend bicameral conference committee deliberations in person.
 At a virtual press conference on Friday, Nov. 13, PBC co-convener Kenneth Isaiah Abante said House leaders had given assurances on the coalition’s eight recommendations, but the group was still waiting for formal measures to carry them out.
 “What’s important to us is not just words or promises, but actions,” Abante said.
 He said the coalition wanted a joint resolution from the House and Senate guaranteeing civil society and media access to the bicameral conference committee, or bicam, which reconciles differences between the two chambers’ versions of the budget.
 “What does concrete action look like for us? Joint resolution stating that the bicameral conference committee will be open to civil society and media,” Abante said, adding that observers should be physically present and not limited to watching livestreams.
 The coalition said it had submitted eight recommendations to House Speaker Faustino “Bojie” Dy III (Isabela-6th) and to members of both the majority and minority blocs.
 These include the public release of supporting documents for budget insertions, identification of the lawmakers who proposed the projects, detailed explanations for changes to agency budgets, and an online system that would allow the public to verify proposed projects.
 The group also called for publication of bicam transcripts and the names of lawmakers who proposed amendments, a shift from patronage-based assistance to rights-based and rules-based social protection, an end to the practice of “parliamentary courtesy” in reviewing the budgets of political offices, and institutionalized civil society participation throughout the budget process.
 Abante said the National Unity Party had signed on to the eight recommendations and that discussions with House members were continuing, but that the coalition had yet to see concrete action on several key proposals.
 The House had announced plans to launch an online platform listing project names, locations, funding allocations, and completion status.
 Dy said on Nov. 9 that the platform would be available to the public in the coming days and that bicam deliberations would be livestreamed.
 At the time of the coalition’s briefing, however, its members said the promised portal was not yet available.
 They also said livestreaming alone would not satisfy their demand for physical access, complete documentation of proceedings, and disclosure of the lawmakers behind amendments.
 The House approved its version of the PHP 7.2-trillion 2027 national budget on third and final reading on Oct. 12, voting 281-13 with one abstention.
 The Senate, meanwhile, has committed to inviting civil society organizations to observe the bicam and to livestreaming its proceedings, according to Sen. Joseph Victor “JV” Ejercito, who chairs the Senate Finance Committee.
 Ejercito said in August that the bicam should not serve as a “backdoor” for last-minute budget insertions, the Philippine Daily Inquirer reported.
 Parliamentary courtesy 
 The PBC raised another concern it said had received less attention: the practice of parliamentary courtesy, which it described as the automatic approval of the budgets of the Office of the President, the Office of the Vice President, and Congress without requiring these offices to fully explain their spending.
 The coalition said it could not find statements of allotments, obligations, and disbursements or financial accountability reports for these offices on their transparency portals.
 It also said the offices were not expected to present their outputs, detailed budget breakdowns, or justifications during budget deliberations.
 “The Congress itself is not willing to subject itself to scrutiny. That in itself is a red flag,” PBC co-convener AJ Montesa said.
 Questioned allocations 
 The group also questioned the proposed increase of nearly PHP 5 billion in the House’s own budget, saying it came as households continued to face rising prices and economic difficulties.
 The House allocation rose from PHP 17.62 billion in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to PHP 22.6 billion in the House-approved version of the General Appropriations Bill.
 The coalition said its sectoral consultations had produced PHP 105 billion in proposals for programs addressing health, education, agriculture, labor, and transportation concerns.
 Only PHP 6.1 billion of these proposals made it into the House version of the budget, it said.
 Among the allocations it questioned was funding for multipurpose buildings, which rose from PHP 43.2 billion in the NEP to PHP 86.3 billion in the House version.
 The group said the increase was difficult to reconcile with the country’s reported shortage of 160,000 classrooms and gaps in health care facilities.
 It also cited nearly PHP 190 billion in about 7,000 infrastructure projects that it said the House had inserted without publicly available supporting documents.
 Citizen monitoring 
 The PBC said it was assembling accountants, auditors, lawyers, budget watchdogs, and civic technology groups to examine the 18,000 infrastructure projects in the 2027 budget.
 It said more than 100 farm-to-market road projects it had flagged were addressed after discussions with the Department of Agriculture, senators, and other government officials.
 The coalition also cited the work of its citizen-monitoring volunteers, who inspected nearly 300 public works projects worth PHP 13 billion across 13 regions.
 Volunteers found defects in 90 of these projects, nine of which the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has since addressed, it said.
 The House expressed support for greater public scrutiny after the PBC briefing.
 On Saturday, Nov. 14, Deputy Speaker Janette Garin (Iloilo-1st) said the chamber welcomed criticism from budget watchdogs and was open to hearing their concerns.
 The PBC said it would continue working with the Senate and executive agencies while pressing House leaders to formalize their commitments.
 “We are willing to work. We are willing to take on the challenge,” Abante said, urging lawmakers to restore public trust through concrete budget reforms.
